title: Wall Street Treads Water as Alphabet, Tesla Earnings Loom and Oil Tops $92
excerpt: Nasdaq futures slip while Dow holds steady ahead of the first Magnificent Seven earnings prints of the season, with surging oil prices and Middle East tensions adding to the uncertainty.
body:
• Nasdaq-100 futures fell 0.77% on Wednesday morning while S&P 500 futures dipped 0.3% and the Dow held near flat, as traders positioned ahead of after-hours earnings from Alphabet and Tesla.
  • Brent crude topped $92 a barrel — up more than $20 from early-July lows — after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran is "not serious" about peace talks, stoking inflation fears and pushing 10-year Treasury yields to 4.64%.
  • Supermicro surged 7% pre-market on a record $60 billion AI-server backlog, lifting Dell 6%, in a sign that data-center spending demand remains robust even as markets question whether it can be monetized.
  • The S&P 500 closed Tuesday at 7,509.20 (+0.89%) and the Nasdaq 100 at 29,155.18 (+1.9%) as chipmakers staged a powerful one-day rebound; those gains are now on the line.

U.S. stocks drifted lower Wednesday morning, surrendering a portion of Tuesday's broad rally as investors locked into a holding pattern ahead of the most consequential earnings reports of the season. Alphabet and Tesla, the first two Magnificent Seven members to open their books this quarter, report after the closing bell — and the results are expected to determine whether the AI-spending trade that has driven markets for two years still has legs.

S&P 500 futures slipped roughly 0.3% to 7,522.50 in pre-market trading. Nasdaq-100 futures led the retreat, down 0.77% at 29,090, while Dow Jones futures were close to flat. The divergence tells you where the anxiety sits: in the megacap growth complex, not the cyclicals.

Tuesday's Rally Built the Ledge

The caution follows a session that looked nothing like this one. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 rose 0.89% to close at 7,509.20, the Dow added 0.74% to 52,224.64, and the Nasdaq 100 jumped 1.9% to 29,155.18. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index surged more than 5% — its best single day in a month — as bargain-hunters piled into chip stocks battered during the prior week's rout.

Memory names did the heavy lifting. Micron and SanDisk each surged more than 12%, SK Hynix rallied 13.75%, and Seagate leapt 11.1%. Of the roughly 66 S&P 500 companies that have reported second-quarter earnings so far, nearly 88% have topped bottom-line estimates, according to FactSet.

"The next two weeks will be a defining stretch for earnings, and not just for tech. The broader message is already clear: companies that fail to clear Wall Street's elevated bar are being punished."

— Bret Kenwell, U.S. investment analyst, eToro

Oil Surges, Inflation Fears Return

Overlaying the earnings anxiety is a geopolitical squeeze. Brent crude topped $92 a barrel Wednesday morning — up more than $20 from early-July lows — after the U.S. struck Iran for a ninth straight day and Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared that Iran is "not serious" about peace talks. West Texas Intermediate jumped more than 3% above $87.

The energy spike has already pushed average U.S. gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and is forcing traders to rethink the Federal Reserve's trajectory. The 10-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.64%, hitting a one-month high, and rate-futures markets now price a roughly 25% probability of a Fed rate hike next Wednesday — up from about 16% at the start of the week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Gold climbed 1.1% to $4,121.20 an ounce as the safe-haven bid returned.

Alphabet: The AI Capex Referendum

Alphabet reports after the close, with a conference call at 4:30 p.m. ET, and the market is treating it as the single most consequential print of the season. The Google parent carries a market capitalization above $4.2 trillion and is expected to deliver earnings and revenue growth exceeding 20% year over year.

The core question is whether surging AI capital expenditure is translating into monetizable revenue. Cloud growth, search advertising resilience, and the capital-spending guidance will all be scrutinized. A raise in capex without matching cloud revenue acceleration would validate the two-week rotation away from AI stocks. A print showing monetization keeping pace with spending could snap the complex back toward recent highs.

Alphabet shares slipped 1.64% on Tuesday even as the Nasdaq rallied — a tell that fast money was trimming exposure before the binary event.

Tesla: Deliveries Beat, but Cash Flow Is the Test

Tesla reports simultaneously, with a live webcast at 5:30 p.m. ET. The setup looks favorable on the surface: Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles in Q2, up 25% from a year ago and roughly 74,000 above consensus, its strongest second quarter ever and first year-over-year delivery growth in two years, according to Electrek.

But the Street's focus will be on cash flow, not units. Capital expenditure tied to the Cybercab robotaxi program, the Optimus humanoid robot, and manufacturing expansion threatens to pressure free cash flow. Automotive gross margins, the robotaxi timeline, and details on the three-row Model Y launch will determine whether the stock holds its recent gains. Full-self-driving progress and any commentary on SpaceX's Starlink integration for the Cybercab — flagged this week by Tesla AI chief Ashok Elluswamy — will get outsized attention.

"The recent correction appears more consistent with a healthy reset following a parabolic advance than a fundamental breakdown in the AI investment theme."

— Adam Turnquist, LPL Financial

Why Indian Diaspora Investors Should Watch

The earnings double-header has direct implications for the large Indian-American investor base with heavy exposure to U.S. tech. Indian-origin professionals at Google, Tesla, and the broader semiconductor ecosystem are watching not just for portfolio signals but for workforce cues — capex guidance from Alphabet and Tesla shapes hiring plans across Silicon Valley. Meanwhile, the oil-price spike ripples through India's economy: the country imports more than 85% of its crude, and every $10 increase in Brent adds roughly 0.4 percentage points to India's wholesale price inflation, putting pressure on the rupee and on Indian equities that many NRIs hold alongside their U.S. portfolios.

What Comes Next

IBM also reports after Wednesday's close, still reeling from a 25% single-day collapse last week on a preliminary earnings miss that rattled the enterprise-software sector. Intel follows Thursday. The week is light on economic data — Thursday brings jobless claims and Friday delivers new-home sales — but the corporate results dominate. With consensus expecting S&P 500 earnings growth of better than 25% year over year this quarter, the risk is asymmetric: beats are priced in, and misses get punished hard. The IBM precedent is fresh.

For now, the market is coiled. The S&P 500's 7,457.69 low from Friday is the level bulls need to defend. Reclaiming and holding above it through Wednesday's reports would signal the rotation is stabilizing. Losing it on a soft Alphabet or Tesla print confirms the two-week unwind has further to run.
